meaning: 'The Benevolent One' — the Bodhisattva who will return as the future Buddha

phonemes.desc: The long diphthong ai — classically a single open 'e'-like glide — carrying the stress: MAI-tre-ya, not mai-TRAY-a.
Dental t with a tapped r and light e — the center of the name, quick and bright.
Palatal y plus short a, the patronymic ending that makes maitrī, 'friendliness,' into a person.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MIGH-tray-yuh' — stress forward on the diphthong; the name is built on maitrī, 'loving-kindness,' so it should sound warm, not martial.

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: maitrī 'friendliness, benevolence,' from mitra 'friend' — Maitreya is the 'Benevolent One,' the abstraction made bodhisattva (Monier-Williams)

kin.label: Pāli
kin.form: Metteyya — the form in which the prophecy of DN 26 names the future Buddha

kin.label: Indo-Iranian
kin.form: mitra, 'friend, contract' — the shared root behind the Vedic god Mitra and Avestan Miθra, friendship divinized in two religions

pronunciation.note: Tier 2: 'Maitreya' is the ASCII-canonical form, with no diacritic-bearing feature lost in plain spelling — the name's restoration lies in its meaning (maitrī, loving-kindness) rather than its letters. Pāli Metteyya preserves the same sounds.

domains.title: Maitreya
domains.subtitle: The Benevolent One — Bodhisattva of the Age to Come
domains.lead: Maitreya is the Buddha of the future — now a bodhisattva enthroned in Tuṣita heaven, waiting for the Dharma's decline to run its course. His name is his program: maitrī, loving-kindness, the first of the four immeasurables — a promise that the wheel, having turned down, will turn up again.

cards.name: The Future Buddha
cards.desc: The prophecy of DN 26: after the Dharma's long decline and renewal, Metteyya will awaken when lifespans reach eighty thousand years.

cards.name: Maitrī, Loving-Kindness
cards.desc: The name made doctrine — the first of the four brahmavihāras, boundless friendliness toward all beings.

cards.name: Tuṣita Heaven
cards.desc: The realm of delight where he waits — and where Śākyamuni waited before his own final birth.

cards.name: The Descent at Ketumatī
cards.desc: The Maitreyavyākaraṇa names his future city, his royal patron Saṅkha, and the tree under which he will wake.

symbols.name: The stūpa in the crown
symbols.meaning: Gandhāran iconography crowns him with a small stūpa — Śākyamuni's relic-shrine marking Maitreya as the appointed successor

symbols.name: The water flask (kamaṇḍalu)
symbols.meaning: The āmra-ghataka of the princely ascetic — the elixir of the future age, medicine for a world whose Dharma has faded

symbols.name: The wheel of Dharma
symbols.meaning: Set beneath his feet on Kushan reliefs — the teaching he will turn again, three assemblies strong

symbols.name: The nāga-puṣpikā tree
symbols.meaning: The tree under which he will awaken in one night at Ketumatī — the future's Bodhi tree, named in the prophecy

symbols.name: The cloth sack (Budai)
symbols.meaning: His Chinese transformation: the laughing monk with his sack of sweets, the future Buddha as abundance and belly-laugh

mythology.lead: Maitreya's mythology is unique in the Buddhist world: it is scheduled but unfulfilled — prophecy rather than biography. The canon names him, the Mahāyāna sūtras detail his future career, and Asia's art made him the most visible future the ancient world ever gave a face.

myths.title: Metteyya at the End of the Decline
myths.text: The oldest prophecy of the future Buddha stands in the Cakkavattisihanāda Sutta (DN 26): after the wheel-turning king Daḷhanemi, greed returns, human life shrinks to ten years — and then, slowly, morality climbs back until people live eighty thousand years. In that age a Buddha named Metteyya will arise, fully awakened, attended by thousands, holding three great assemblies beneath a pavilion — and the wheel will turn a fourth time in this eon. Later Pāli texts place him now in Tuṣita heaven, where Śākyamuni himself waited before his final birth. The myth is the Buddhist answer to a hard fact — every Buddha's teaching decays — and its answer is not despair but schedule: the wheel turns down and up again, and the next teacher is already named, already enthroned, already waiting.

myths.title: The Descent at Ketumatī
myths.text: The Sanskrit tradition gives the future a city and a plot. The Maitreyavyākaraṇa — transmitted within the Divyāvadāna and translated repeatedly into Chinese and Tibetan — describes Maitreya's birth in splendid Ketumatī, when the wheel-turning king Saṅkha rules, lifespans run to eighty thousand years, and the Dharma has been forgotten. Born to the brahmin Subrahma, he will leave his palace by the four gates, meet an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a renunciant — the very sights that unseated Śākyamuni — and awaken beneath a nāga-puṣpikā tree in a single night. The sūtra's sharpest promise is addressed to its hearers: those who receive this prophecy will meet Maitreya face to face. The myth makes eschatology personal — salvation not as catastrophe but as a scheduled appointment with a named teacher, and a ticket any listener can hold.

myths.title: The Earliest Future on Earth
myths.text: Maitreya is among the very first bodhisattvas to receive cult — earlier than most of the Mahāyāna pantheon. Gandhāran art of the Kuṣāṇa centuries (2nd–3rd c. CE) already shows him in the dress of a princely ascetic: stūpa in the crown, water flask in hand, sometimes teaching with a wheel at his feet. The emblem choice is theology in stone — the stūpa names him successor, the flask the medicine of the age to come; inscriptions call him simply Metr, the Middle Indic form. Along the Silk Road his cult became geography: caravan towns from Khotan to Dunhuang painted his descent, and devotion to his coming seeded messianic movements whenever the age grew dark — most famously in China's rebellions of the sixth and tenth centuries, when "Maitreya has descended" was a battle cry. The meaning of the images: a religion that put its future in human shape, standing where the caravans could see him.

myths.title: Budai, the Laughing Maitreya
myths.text: In China the austere future Buddha was re-imagined as a fat, laughing monk. From the tenth century onward, the eccentric wanderer Budai (布袋, "Cloth Sack") — a historical monk of the Wuyue kingdom, d. 917, who carried sweets and toys for children and was believed to be Maitreya in disguise — replaced the princely bodhisattva in the popular imagination. The Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp (1004) preserves his sayings, and his image, belly bared at the temple gate, became the most reproduced Buddhist figure in the world after the seated Śākyamuni. The transformation is doctrinal as much as comic: Maitreya's age is one of abundance and eighty-thousand-year lives, so his sign is a belly, not an emaciated rib-cage — a prophecy of plenty arriving as laughter, standing at the threshold of every Chinese monastery to remind the poor that the next age will be fed.

lore.syncretism: Maitreya's reception is the strangest career of any bodhisattva. In India he absorbed the iconography of a future world-ruler — crowned, princely, seated European-style with pendant legs, a god of the age to come. Central Asian Islam met him on the cave walls of Dunhuang and kept his silhouette in manuscript illumination. China fused him with the folk saint Budai and made the laughing fat monk his universal form; Korea and Japan inherited both the regal Maitreza/Miroku of the temples and the round-bellied Hotei of the gate. In Japan, Miroku became the focus of sundered-age hope — the mappō centuries looked to him as the one who comes when Śākyamuni's law has faded. Modern scholarship (Sponberg & Hardacre's Maitreya, the Future Buddha) treats him as the closest Buddhism came to a messiah: not a savior from outside history, but its next chapter.
lore.culturalLegacy: No Buddhist figure is more painted. The colossal Maitreya niches of Bamiyan — one of the two great Buddhas was identified with him — dominated the Silk Road until their destruction in 2001; the third phase of Borobudur and the cave temples of Bingling and Maijishan climb toward his heaven. The Anāgatavaṃsa kept his cult alive in Sri Lanka, and Burmese and Thai Buddhism still recite the prophecy of his coming. In East Asia, Budai-Maitreya smiles from restaurant windows and temple gates, and the word for his sack of plenty entered the language of New Year greetings. The laughing form is the deeper truth of the name: a future guaranteed not by wrath but by friendliness — maitrī itself, scheduled to arrive.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Every religion promises an end; Buddhism alone promises a sequel. Maitreya is the argument that decline is not the last chapter — that the Dharma, having dimmed, will be re-taught in full, by a teacher already named, already enthroned in the heaven of delight. The figure dissolves despair without denying decay: the wheel does turn down, and it turns up again.

He is also the most human of the great bodhisattvas because his career is still open. The Buddha's story is closed and perfect; Maitreya's is a promise with a waiting room, and the tradition placed Śākyamuni himself in that room before his final birth. To venerate Maitreya is to admit that one's own age is incomplete — and to refuse to treat incompleteness as defeat. The future Buddha is Buddhism's answer to the oldest anxiety: what if it all ends with us? Not, says the prophecy. It ends, and it begins again, kinder.

lore.archaeology: Maitreya is among the earliest bodhisattvas imaged in stone. Kuṣāṇa-period Gandhāra (2nd–3rd c. CE) gives him his classic type: princely jewelry, stūpa-in-crown, water flask, the wheel at his feet; Mathurā workshops add the dharma-cakra-mudrā preaching pose. The colossi scale up along the Silk Road — the 55-meter Bamiyan east niche (6th–7th c., destroyed 2001) and the 27-meter Maitreya of Bingling Si's cave 171. In China the earliest datable Maitreya image (the gilt bronze of 443 CE in the Asian Art Museum tradition) and the great Northern Wei votive steles mark the cult's imperial sponsorship. Inscriptions from Swat to Khotan name him Metr — the future Buddha already receiving donations in his own lifetime's echo.
